title: Injection Every 2 Months (Cabotegravir)
tagline: A shot at your provider's office every 2 months - no daily pills to remember
keyTakeaways: Get a shot every 2 months at your provider's office - no daily pill needed
Shown to be even more effective than daily pills in clinical studies
Great option if you don't want to think about HIV prevention every day
Injection site soreness is the most common side effect and usually goes away quickly
Important: If you stop, the medicine stays in your body for a long time - you'll need a plan to stay protected during that period

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Injectable PrEP with cabotegravir (brand name Apretude) is a shot you get at your healthcare provider's office every 2 months. Instead of remembering a daily pill, you simply show up for your appointments and your provider takes care of the rest. This option became available in 2021 and has been a game-changer for people who prefer not to take a daily pill.
keyPoints: A shot in the buttock muscle every 2 months
No pills to take at home between visits
Approved for adults and adolescents weighing at least 77 pounds (35 kg)
Given by a healthcare provider at a clinic or doctor's office

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: Cabotegravir is a long-acting medicine that belongs to a class of drugs called integrase inhibitors. When injected into the muscle of your buttock, it forms a small depot (a slow-release reservoir) that gradually releases medicine into your bloodstream over weeks. This keeps protective levels of the drug in your body between appointments, blocking HIV from being able to copy itself if you're exposed.
keyPoints: The medicine is injected into the gluteal muscle (buttock)
It slowly releases from the injection site over time
Blocks a key enzyme HIV needs to reproduce (called integrase)
Maintains protective drug levels between your every-2-month visits

sections.title: Dosing Schedule
sections.content: Getting started with injectable PrEP involves a few steps. First, you'll take a daily oral tablet of cabotegravir for about one month to make sure you tolerate the medication well. Then you'll get your first injection, followed by a second injection one month later. After that, you'll come in every 2 months for your ongoing injections.
keyPoints: Step 1: Take a daily cabotegravir tablet for about 4 weeks (the oral lead-in period)
Step 2: Get your first injection at your provider's office
Step 3: Return 1 month later for your second injection
Step 4: Continue getting injections every 2 months after that
Your provider will also do HIV testing at each visit

callouts.title: Why the oral lead-in?
callouts.text: The oral lead-in period lets you try the medicine in pill form first. This way, if you have any side effects, they'll go away quickly when you stop the pill. Once you know you tolerate it well, you can move on to the long-acting injection with confidence.

sections.title: Effectiveness
sections.content: In large clinical trials, injectable cabotegravir was shown to be even more effective than daily oral PrEP at preventing HIV. This is likely because getting a shot removes the challenge of remembering to take a pill every day - you get your protection built in at each visit, with no daily effort required between appointments.
keyPoints: Clinical studies showed cabotegravir injections were superior to daily oral PrEP
The higher effectiveness is likely because there's no chance of forgetting a daily dose
Protection is maintained between appointments as long as you stay on schedule
One of the most effective HIV prevention methods available

sections.title: Side Effects
sections.content: The most common side effect is a reaction at the injection site - soreness, swelling, or tenderness in your buttock where you got the shot. For most people, this is mild and goes away within a few days. Some people also experience mild headache, fever, or fatigue after the injection.
keyPoints: Injection site reactions (soreness, hardness, or swelling) are the most common side effect
These reactions are usually mild to moderate and improve within a few days
Reactions tend to get milder with each subsequent injection
Some people feel mild flu-like symptoms for a day or two after the shot
Serious side effects are rare

callouts.title: Managing injection site discomfort
callouts.text: Applying a warm compress or gently massaging the area can help with soreness. Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can also help. Most people say the discomfort is very manageable.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.content: To start injectable PrEP, you'll need to see a provider who offers this option. Not all clinics carry injectable PrEP yet, so you may need to check with your provider or find a clinic that offers it. Here's what to expect when you're getting set up:
keyPoints: You'll get an HIV test to confirm you're HIV-negative
Your provider will review your health history and any medications you take
You'll start with the oral lead-in period (about 4 weeks of daily pills)
After the lead-in, you'll get your first injection at the clinic
Plan to stay at the clinic for about 15-30 minutes after your first injection for monitoring

callouts.title: Finding a provider
callouts.text: Not all clinics offer injectable PrEP yet. If your current provider doesn't offer it, you can search for clinics near you that do. The Resources section of this tool has links to help you find providers.

sections.title: Appointment Windows
sections.content: Life happens, and sometimes you might not be able to come in exactly on the scheduled date. There's some flexibility built in - you have a window of about 7 days before or after your scheduled date to get your injection and still maintain protection.
keyPoints: Your target is every 2 months (about 8 weeks) between injections
You have a window of plus or minus 7 days from your scheduled date
If you're more than 7 days late, talk to your provider - you may need additional steps
Set reminders ahead of time so you don't miss your window

callouts.title: Stay on schedule
callouts.text: Schedule your next appointment before you leave the clinic. Setting a calendar reminder a week before your appointment can help make sure you don't miss your window.

sections.title: Stopping Cabotegravir Injections
sections.content: This is one of the most important things to understand about injectable PrEP. Because cabotegravir is a long-acting medication, it stays in your body for a long time after your last injection - sometimes 12 months or longer. During this "tail" period, drug levels are slowly dropping but aren't high enough to fully protect you. This creates a window where you could be at risk of getting HIV, and if infected, the virus could develop resistance to the medication.
keyPoints: Cabotegravir stays in your body for 12 months or more after your last injection
During this time, drug levels may be too low to fully protect you
You MUST use another form of protection during this tail period
Talk to your provider about switching to oral PrEP or using condoms consistently
Never stop injectable PrEP without talking to your provider first

callouts.title: The long tail - please read this carefully
callouts.text: Unlike the daily pill, you cannot simply stop cabotegravir injections and walk away. The medicine lingers in your body at decreasing levels for a year or more. During this tail period, you need another form of HIV prevention (like oral PrEP or condoms) to stay protected. Your provider will help you make a transition plan. This is one of the most important things to consider when choosing this option.

sections.title: Cost & Access
sections.content: Injectable PrEP is covered by most insurance plans, and there are assistance programs available if cost is a concern. Because the injections are given at a clinic, the cost includes both the medication and the administration fee.
keyPoints: Most insurance plans (including Medicaid in many states) cover injectable PrEP
ViiV Healthcare (the manufacturer) offers a patient assistance program for those who qualify
The medication itself plus the clinic visit for the injection are both part of the cost
If you have insurance, copay assistance may be available through ViiV's program
Community health centers may offer injectable PrEP on a sliding fee scale

callouts.title: Help with costs
callouts.text: If you're worried about paying for injectable PrEP, ask your provider's office about assistance programs. ViiV Healthcare offers support for eligible patients, and many clinics can help you navigate your options.

sections.title: Common Questions
sections.content: Here are answers to some of the questions people ask most often about injectable PrEP with cabotegravir.
keyPoints: Q: Does the injection hurt? - A: You'll feel a pinch and some pressure during the injection. Most people say it's very manageable. Soreness afterward is common but usually mild.
Q: Which side do I get the shot on? - A: Your provider will alternate between the left and right buttock at each visit.
Q: Can I exercise after getting the injection? - A: Yes, but you may want to take it easy on your glutes for a day or two if the area is sore.

Q: What if I decide I don't like the injections? - A: You can switch to oral PrEP or another option. Just talk to your provider so they can help you transition safely, especially because of the long tail period.

Q: Can I get the injection if I'm pregnant or planning to become pregnant? - A: Talk to your provider. Injectable cabotegravir may be an option during pregnancy, but your provider will help weigh the benefits and considerations for your situation.
Q: Will anyone know I'm getting PrEP injections? - A: Your PrEP use is confidential. Since you get the injection at a clinic and don't have pills at home, some people find this option more private.
